guest.bio_context: Daniel Harms moved to Dunedin in 2011 from Sydney, where he worked with a recruitment company after initially selling in London following university. He founded Platinum Recruitment in 2014, starting from a bedroom in Mosgill with no clients or candidates, and has since grown it into a multi-location firm operating across New Zealand. Beyond business, he is involved with local governance initiatives, the Dunedin Fringe Arts Trust, and the Dunedin Wildlife Hospital.

context.transcript_excerpt: Coming up on the Otago Opportunity, we're talking to Daniel Harms from Platinum Recruitment about the current challenges in the job market, future trends and maybe some advice. This is the Otago Opportunity, a limited series look at the future of our province. I'm your host, Pauline Moore, and in this series, we're taking the policies of the Opportunity Party and moving them out of the Wellington think tank and into our own backyard here in Dunedin. Each week we'll hear from local business owners, students and families about how a tax reset or a citizens assembly would actually impact their daily lives. It's not about the politics, it's about the future of the place we call home. Welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Hi ora and welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Joining me today is Dave Bainbridge-Zafar, the opportunity candidate for Dunedin, and our guest, Daniel Harms, the founder and director of Platinum Recruitment here in Dunedin. Welcome. Kia ora. Kia ora. Thanks for the welcome, Paulie. Daniel, can you just tell us a little bit about Planet Recruitment as a business, how you started and what the reason was for starting a business like this? yeah so uh i i've always worked in recruitment um so when i left uh university as a as a graduate um much like most people left with a little bit of debt and uh and i always had dreams of becoming a wildlife ranger or something like that but uh you know good good good old debt made me choose a different path or and so i ended up selling stuff in london uh from the uk originally and then sort of naturally gravitated into the world of recruitment. And that's allowed me to travel the world and ended up in Sydney, working with a recruitment company over there, where I met the mother of my children, who is from Dunedin. And so when we decided to do the family thing, we headed this way. And I think that was 2011, headed over here and then started the business in 2014. And, you know, I always had this vision that I would be part of a business. I just didn't necessarily think I would found the business. It took a relationship first approach that really sort of bridged that gap between client and candidate and tried to do a little bit more rather than just being a sort of transactional recruitment type firm. And actually be in a position to be able to give back. And the fact that we're here in Dunedin 12 years later doing exactly that is great. But I'm surrounded by awesome people who support me, support that vision and share that vision. So is that what you think makes your agency unique, that it's very much relationship focused? I think it's one of the things. Yeah, it's one of the things. Certainly, you know, we do take that relationship first approach. And I think we're relatively well known locally for taking that relationship first approach. Recruitment as a business, as an industry, it's an unregulated industry. It's a global industry. It's worth billions of dollars. And so sometimes I think it can be quite transactional. And I've always wanted to move away from the transactional side of things and still recognize that we're a sales business. We're a professional services business, but we want to be in a position to be able to do more and offer more. Can you tell us what that first week of your business was like? Yeah, yeah. So cast the mind back to 2014, the 1st of April in a bedroom in Mosgill, opened up my laptop computer and turned on my CRM and my database and on it was absolutely nothing. No clients, no candidates, just me, a telephone and a willingness, I guess, to do some good. And yeah, so kind of launched into it. And from there, started about building up my candidate database, building up my client contacts. I think it was six months or so later that I managed to move out of the bedroom and into an office into Dunedin. and shortly after that, hired three people all at the same time, one of whom's still with me, but the other two I'm still close to. So, yeah, it's been an awesome,

pending_qa.q: What advice would a recruitment leader give to university graduates trying to compete for limited jobs in smaller regional economies?
pending_qa.r: Harms encourages students to stand out by getting involved in wider community initiatives beyond their degree or qualification, and to consider building their own startup rather than waiting for corporate jobs. He highlights that Startup Dunedin and well-connected local mentors can support graduates in commercializing solutions to real problems.

pending_qa.q: What government policy changes would best support private business growth in a region heavily dependent on public sector employment?
pending_qa.r: Harms advocates for growing investment in the startup ecosystem rather than offering tax breaks to attract external businesses, which he argues is ineffective. He wants more support for the startup world and increased investment in that space to help Dunedin build its own private sector capacity to 40-50 percent of total employment.

pending_qa.q: What is the most rewarding aspect of running a recruitment business focused on relationship-driven placements?
pending_qa.r: Harms views his business as another child in his preteen years with wonderful growing pains and excitement. He is most proud of contributing to the personal and professional growth of people within the business, and solving problems by placing people into jobs they might not have known existed, creating a win-win dynamic that helps both candidates and employers.
